note: Notes for the 9 PHY101 topics. Topic IDs match phy101_questions.json exactly so these merge into the same course document. Each note is written to be read start-to-finish in a few minutes, with the one formula/idea most relevant to the practice questions called out explicitly.

topics.title: Kinematics — Motion in a Straight Line
topics.notes:
Kinematics describes motion without asking what caused it — no forces, just position, velocity, and acceleration as functions of time. Displacement x(t) is the starting point; velocity is how fast x changes (v = dx/dt), and acceleration is how fast velocity changes (a = dv/dt). If you're given x(t) as a polynomial, you differentiate twice to get acceleration at any instant — this is the most common trap-and-release pattern in past questions: students forget to differentiate twice, or plug in t before taking the second derivative.

For constant acceleration (the far more common case in exam questions), you don't need calculus — three equations cover almost everything: v = u + at, s = ut + ½at², and v² = u² + 2as. The trick is always identifying which three of the five variables (u, v, a, s, t) you're given, and picking the equation missing the one you don't need.

Projectile motion is kinematics in two dimensions treated as two independent one-dimensional problems: horizontal velocity never changes (no horizontal force, ignoring air resistance), while vertical velocity changes at g = 9.8 m/s² (or 10 m/s² depending on the paper). The resultant speed at any point is found by combining the two components with Pythagoras — this shows up constantly in past questions asking for 'speed after t seconds' when something is thrown horizontally or at an angle.

KEY FORMULA: v² = u² + 2as — this single equation solves the majority of 'find the velocity at a certain point' questions without needing to know the time at all.

topics.title: Newton's Laws, Forces & Connected Bodies
topics.notes:
Newton's three laws are the foundation everything else in mechanics builds on. The first law says an object moving at constant velocity has zero net force on it — this is a trap in exam questions that describe a car 'moving at constant speed' and then ask for the net force: the answer is always 0N, no calculation needed. The second law, F = ma, is the workhorse formula — most force problems reduce to identifying every force acting on a body, summing them (with correct signs for direction), and setting the result equal to ma.

Connected bodies — blocks joined by strings over pulleys — are one of the most-tested setups in past papers. The key insight: both bodies share the same magnitude of acceleration (the string is inextensible), so you can treat the whole system as one equation. For a classic two-mass pulley system (Atwood machine), the acceleration is a = (m₂−m₁)g/(m₁+m₂) when m₂ is heavier and falling. The tension in the string is not simply the weight of either mass — you have to solve for it using either body's individual equation of motion once you know the acceleration.

Friction problems add one more force to track: the maximum static friction is f = μN, where N is the normal force (not necessarily equal to weight — check the geometry, especially for objects on inclines or pressed against vertical surfaces). A body 'remains static' exactly when the applied force doesn't exceed this maximum.

KEY FORMULA: F = ma, and for a two-mass pulley system, a = (m₂−m₁)g/(m₁+m₂).

topics.title: Work, Energy & Power
topics.notes:
Work is done when a force causes displacement in the direction of that force: W = F·d·cosθ, where θ is the angle between the force and the direction of motion. The cosθ term is where most mistakes happen — if a force is applied at an angle to the direction of travel, only the component of force along the direction of motion does work. Read the question carefully for whether the angle is measured from the horizontal or the vertical, since that flips cos and sin.

A closed-loop path (returning to the starting point) does zero net work against a conservative force like gravity, regardless of how long or winding the path was — this catches students who instinctively multiply force by total distance traveled instead of net displacement.

The work-energy theorem connects this directly to kinetic energy: the net work done on a body equals its change in kinetic energy, W = ΔKE = ½mv_f² − ½mv_i². This is often faster than working through kinematics equations when a question gives you speeds and asks for force or work directly.

Power is simply the rate at which work is done: P = W/t, or equivalently P = F·v for a body moving at constant velocity against a resisting force (very common in 'car engine power' questions — at steady speed, engine force equals the opposing friction/resistance force).

KEY FORMULA: W = ΔKE = ½mv_f² − ½mv_i², and P = F·v at constant velocity.

topics.title: Momentum, Impulse & Collisions
topics.notes:
Momentum (p = mv) is a vector — direction matters as much as magnitude, and this is where most errors creep in. When combining momenta of two bodies moving in opposite directions, one of them must be negative. Always fix a positive direction first and stick to it through the whole problem.

Impulse is the change in momentum, and it equals the average force multiplied by the time of contact: Impulse = FΔt = m(v_f − v_i). This is the formula behind every 'ball hits a wall' or 'bat hits a ball' question — figure out the momentum before and after (careful with signs if the object rebounds), and divide by the contact time to get average force.

Collisions come in two flavors that matter for past questions: momentum is always conserved in any collision (nothing external acting), but kinetic energy is only conserved in a perfectly elastic collision. The coefficient of restitution, e = (relative speed of separation)/(relative speed of approach), measures how 'bouncy' a collision is — e=1 is perfectly elastic, e=0 means the objects stick together. In real exam numbers, always sanity-check that your computed e falls between 0 and 1; if it doesn't, double-check your before/after velocity assignments, since a value outside that range usually means a sign error.

KEY FORMULA: Impulse = m(v_f − v_i) = FΔt.

topics.title: Circular Motion & Gravitation
topics.notes:
An object moving in a circle at constant speed is still accelerating — the direction of its velocity keeps changing, and that acceleration points toward the center of the circle (centripetal acceleration), with magnitude a = v²/r = ω²r. This is a conceptual trap in past questions: 'constant speed' does not mean 'zero acceleration' when the path is curved.

For satellites and orbits, the same centripetal idea combines with Newton's law of gravitation: the gravitational force provides exactly the centripetal force needed to keep a satellite in orbit. Working through GMm/r² = mv²/r and simplifying gives orbital speed v = √(GM/r) — notice this means satellites farther from earth move slower, not faster, which is another common exam trap.

Kepler's second law (equal areas in equal times) is the reason elliptical orbits have varying speed: a satellite moves fastest at perigee (closest approach) and slowest at apogee (farthest point). Past papers test this as a pure concept question repeatedly — memorize that pairing (fast-close, slow-far) rather than the derivation.

Be careful distinguishing Kepler's three actual laws (elliptical orbits, equal areas, period² ∝ radius³) from Newton's law of universal gravitation (F = GMm/r²) — past papers include 'which is NOT one of Kepler's laws' questions that hinge on recognizing gravitation itself isn't one of the three.

KEY FORMULA: v = √(GM/r) for circular orbital speed.

topics.title: Rotational Motion & Moment of Inertia
topics.notes:
Moment of inertia (I) is rotation's version of mass — it measures how hard it is to change an object's rotational motion, and unlike mass, it depends on how the object's mass is distributed relative to the axis of rotation. Standard shapes have standard formulas worth memorizing outright: solid sphere I=(2/5)mr², solid cylinder/disk I=(1/2)mr², thin ring I=mr². Past questions almost always give you the shape directly, so the calculation is just plugging into the right formula — the actual skill being tested is recognizing which formula applies.

Rotational kinetic energy mirrors the translational formula: KE = ½Iω² (compare to ½mv² for straight-line motion). For an object that's rolling without slipping (like a wheel), it has both translational and rotational kinetic energy simultaneously, and you add them: KE_total = ½mv² + ½Iω². Since ω = v/r for rolling without slipping, this combination simplifies neatly for standard shapes — for a solid cylinder rolling, it works out to KE_total = ¾mv².

Angular quantities (θ, ω, α) relate to linear ones exactly the way you'd expect: v=ωr, a=αr — treat angular kinematics equations as a direct translation of the linear ones (ω = ω₀+αt, etc.).

KEY FORMULA: KE_rotational = ½Iω², and for rolling: KE_total = ½mv² + ½Iω².

topics.title: Simple Harmonic Motion
topics.notes:
Simple harmonic motion is any oscillation where the restoring force (and therefore acceleration) is proportional to displacement from equilibrium and points back toward it: a = −ω²x. This single relationship is the definition of SHM and the source of every formula in the topic.

The velocity at any displacement x, given amplitude A, is v = ω√(A² − x²) — notice velocity is maximum (v_max = ωA) at the center (x=0) and zero at the extremes (x=±A), which matches intuition: a pendulum or spring moves fastest passing through equilibrium and momentarily stops at the top of its swing.

Angular frequency ω connects to the more familiar frequency f and period T by ω = 2πf = 2π/T. Past questions frequently give you frequency in Hz and expect you to convert to ω before using any of the SHM formulas — forgetting this conversion is the single most common arithmetic error in this topic.

For a simple pendulum specifically, period depends only on length and gravity: T = 2π√(L/g) — notably NOT on mass or amplitude (for small swings). This is why 'what happens to the period if mass is doubled' questions always have the same answer: nothing changes.

KEY FORMULA: v = ω√(A² − x²), where ω = 2πf.

topics.title: Kinetic Theory of Gases
topics.notes:
The kinetic theory of gases models a gas as a huge number of tiny particles in constant, random motion, colliding elastically with each other and the container walls. From this simple picture, you can derive real, measurable quantities like pressure and temperature — this is the conceptual bridge between the microscopic (individual molecules) and macroscopic (pressure gauges, thermometers) worlds.

The root-mean-square speed of gas molecules, v_rms = √(3P/ρ) = √(3RT/M), tells you the typical speed of molecules given pressure and density (or temperature and molar mass). This is usually a direct plug-in-the-numbers calculation once you've identified which form of the formula matches what the question gives you — density-based or temperature-based.

Several 'postulates of kinetic theory' appear repeatedly as concept questions: molecules are in random motion, they're far apart compared to their own size, and — critically — collisions are perfectly elastic (this is often the false option that questions test, since real inelastic collisions would let the gas lose energy and settle down, which contradicts a gas maintaining constant pressure).

Dimensional analysis also shows up here — knowing that pressure has dimension ML⁻¹T⁻² (force per area) lets you check quantities like bulk modulus, which shares the same dimension since it's also a pressure-like quantity (stress divided by dimensionless strain).

KEY FORMULA: v_rms = √(3P/ρ).
